subject.name: Chemistry
subject.description: Cambridge International AS & A Level Chemistry. AS Level students take Papers 1 and 2 (topics 1–22); A Level students also take Paper 4 (topics 23–37). Calculations use values from the Cambridge Data Booklet. The practical papers (3 and 5) are not included. The questions are original practice questions written in the style of Cambridge papers, not reproduced past paper material.

topics.title: An introduction to AS Level organic chemistry
Chemical energetics
topics.summary: Lattice energy, Born–Haber cycles, entropy and Gibbs free energy.

topics.title: Electrochemistry
topics.summary: Electrolysis, standard electrode potentials, the Nernst equation.

topics.title: Equilibria
topics.summary: Acids and bases, pH, buffers, solubility product, partition coefficients.

topics.title: Reaction kinetics
topics.summary: Rate equations, orders, half-life, mechanisms, catalysis.

topics.title: Group 2
topics.summary: Thermal stability and solubility of Group 2 compounds.

topics.title: Chemistry of transition elements
topics.summary: Properties, complexes, colour and redox of transition elements.

topics.title: An introduction to A Level organic chemistry
topics.summary: Formulae and isomerism, including optical isomerism and arenes.

topics.title: Nitrogen compounds
topics.summary: Amines, phenylamine, azo compounds, amides, amino acids.

topics.title: Analytical techniques
topics.summary: Thin-layer and gas chromatography, carbon-13 and proton NMR.

parts.prompt: How many neutrons are in the ion ⁸¹Br⁻?

parts.examinerComment: Electrons have a much smaller mass than protons but the same size of charge, so they are deflected much more.

parts.prompt: What mass of magnesium oxide is formed when {m} g of magnesium is burned completely in oxygen? (Aᵣ: Mg = 24.3, O = 16.0)
parts.examinerComment: Moles of MgO = moles of Mg. Option A is only the mass of oxygen that combines with the magnesium.

parts.prompt: Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms?
parts.examinerComment: 9.0 g of water is 0.50 mol of molecules, each containing three atoms, so 1.5 mol of atoms. The others each contain 1.0 mol of atoms.

parts.prompt: {v} cm³ of {c} mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, is exactly neutralised by aqueous sodium hydroxide. How many moles of NaOH reacted?
parts.examinerComment: Sulfuric acid is diprotic: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Remember to convert cm³ to dm³.

parts.prompt: Which molecule contains polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
parts.examinerComment: CO₂ is linear, so the two bond dipoles cancel. Water and ammonia are bent and pyramidal, so their dipoles do not cancel.

parts.prompt: What is the shape of a sulfur hexafluoride molecule, SF₆?
parts.examinerComment: Six bonding pairs and no lone pairs around sulfur give an octahedral shape with 90° bond angles.

parts.prompt: Which compound contains a dative covalent (coordinate) bond?
parts.examinerComment: In NH₄⁺ the lone pair on nitrogen is donated to an H⁺ ion. Once formed, all four N–H bonds are identical.

parts.prompt: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?

markingPoints.text: A – high temperature and low pressure

parts.examinerComment: At high temperature and low pressure the molecules are far apart and moving fast, so intermolecular forces and molecular volume are negligible.

parts.prompt: What volume is occupied by {n} mol of an ideal gas at {T} K and {p} kPa? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
parts.examinerComment: With p in kPa, V = nRT/p gives the volume directly in dm³. Option B uses the Celsius temperature.

parts.prompt: Which change doubles the volume of a fixed mass of an ideal gas?

options.text: doubling the Kelvin temperature at constant pressure
doubling the Celsius temperature at constant pressure
doubling the pressure at constant temperature
halving the Kelvin temperature at constant pressure

markingPoints.text: A – doubling the Kelvin temperature at constant pressure

parts.examinerComment: V ∝ T only when T is measured in kelvin. Doubling the pressure would halve the volume.

parts.prompt: The standard enthalpy changes of combustion of carbon, hydrogen and ethane, C₂H₆, are −394, −286 and {c} kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. What is the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethane, in kJ mol⁻¹?
parts.examinerComment: ΔHf = 2(−394) + 3(−286) − ΔHc(C₂H₆). Option B has the sign reversed; option C uses one mole of each element.

parts.prompt: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol?
parts.examinerComment: Formation is from the elements in their standard states, forming one mole of the compound.

parts.prompt: For H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), ΔH = −{d} kJ mol⁻¹. The bond energies of H–H and Cl–Cl are 436 and 242 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the bond energy of H–Cl, in kJ mol⁻¹?
parts.examinerComment: Bonds broken − bonds made = ΔH, so 678 − 2E(H–Cl) = −{d}. Remember that two H–Cl bonds are formed.

parts.prompt: In which reaction is nitrogen oxidised?
parts.examinerComment: In B the oxidation number of nitrogen rises from −3 to +2. In A it falls from 0 to −3; in C and D it does not change.

parts.prompt: In the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, which species is the oxidising agent?
parts.examinerComment: Fe³⁺ gains electrons (is reduced), so it oxidises the iodide ions.

parts.prompt: How many moles of electrons are needed to reduce one mole of VO₂⁺ ions to V²⁺ ions?
parts.examinerComment: Vanadium in VO₂⁺ has oxidation number +5, so three electrons per ion are needed to reach +2.

parts.prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia?
parts.examinerComment: There are fewer moles of gas on the right, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right. A catalyst does not change the yield.

parts.prompt: What are the units of Kc for the equilibrium 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)?
parts.examinerComment: Kc = [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂]); the units are (mol dm⁻³)⁻¹ = mol⁻¹ dm³.

parts.prompt: In the equilibrium HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which two species are a conjugate acid–base pair?
parts.examinerComment: A conjugate pair differs by one proton. The other pair is H₂O and H₃O⁺.

parts.prompt: Why does a small increase in temperature cause a large increase in the rate of a reaction?

options.text: Many more molecules have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
The activation energy of the reaction decreases.
The frequency of collisions increases greatly.
The enthalpy change of the reaction becomes more negative.

markingPoints.text: A – Many more molecules have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.

parts.examinerComment: The increase in collision frequency is small; the main effect is the larger area under the Boltzmann curve beyond Eₐ.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes how a heterogeneous catalyst works?

options.text: It is in the same phase as the reactants and forms an intermediate in solution.
Reactants are adsorbed onto its surface, which weakens bonds and provides a route with a lower activation energy.
It increases the energy of the reactant molecules.
It shifts the position of equilibrium towards the products.

markingPoints.text: B – Reactants are adsorbed onto its surface, which weakens bonds and provides a route with a lower activation energy.

parts.examinerComment: Adsorption, reaction on the surface and desorption is the typical sequence for a heterogeneous catalyst such as iron in the Haber process.

parts.prompt: Which change increases the frequency of collisions without changing the proportion of molecules with energy greater than the activation energy?

options.text: increasing the concentration of a reactant
increasing the temperature and adding a catalyst

markingPoints.text: A – increasing the concentration of a reactant

parts.examinerComment: Concentration changes the number of particles per unit volume, not their energy distribution.

parts.prompt: Which oxide of a Period 3 element is amphoteric?
parts.examinerComment: Aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis. SiO₂ is acidic, reacting only with hot concentrated alkali.

parts.prompt: Which Period 3 element has the highest melting point?
parts.examinerComment: Silicon has a giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken.

parts.prompt: In which oxide does the Period 3 element have an oxidation number of +5?
parts.examinerComment: P₄O₁₀: 4x = 20, so x = +5. Sulfur in SO₃ is +6.

parts.prompt: Which Group 2 sulfate is the least soluble in water?
parts.examinerComment: The solubility of the sulfates decreases down the group; BaSO₄ is used as the test precipitate for sulfate ions.

parts.prompt: What is formed when magnesium is heated in steam?
parts.examinerComment: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂. With cold water, magnesium reacts very slowly to give the hydroxide.

parts.prompt: Which compound is used in agriculture to raise the pH of acidic soil?
parts.examinerComment: Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is a base, so it neutralises acids in the soil.

parts.prompt: What colour is a solution of iodine in cyclohexane?
parts.examinerComment: Iodine is brown in water but violet (purple) in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane.

parts.prompt: Which halide ion reduces concentrated sulfuric acid to hydrogen sulfide?
parts.examinerComment: Iodide is the strongest reducing agent of the halide ions; bromide only reduces the acid as far as SO₂.

parts.prompt: A hot glass rod is placed in a sample of each hydrogen halide. Which one decomposes most readily, giving a coloured vapour?
parts.examinerComment: The H–I bond is the longest and weakest, so HI is the least thermally stable; violet iodine vapour forms.

parts.prompt: Which equation shows ammonia acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base?
parts.examinerComment: Ammonia accepts a proton from water. In C the ammonium ion is the proton donor.

parts.prompt: Ammonium chloride is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What is the gas produced and its effect on damp red litmus paper?
parts.examinerComment: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. Ammonia is alkaline, so it turns damp red litmus blue.

parts.prompt: What is the role of nitrogen dioxide in the atmospheric oxidation of sulfur dioxide?

options.text: It acts as a catalyst for the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃.
It reduces SO₃ back to SO₂.
It reacts with SO₂ to give sulfuric acid directly.

markingPoints.text: A – It acts as a catalyst for the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃.

parts.examinerComment: NO₂ + SO₂ → NO + SO₃, then NO + ½O₂ → NO₂, so NO₂ is regenerated.

parts.prompt: What is the molecular formula of 2-methylbutan-2-ol?
parts.examinerComment: Butane chain (4 C) plus a methyl group gives five carbons; it is a saturated alcohol, CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH.

parts.prompt: What type of bond fission occurs in the initiation step of a free-radical substitution reaction?
parts.examinerComment: Each atom keeps one electron from the bond, forming two radicals.

parts.prompt: Which compound shows geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism?
parts.examinerComment: Each carbon of the C=C in pent-2-ene has two different groups attached. In C, one carbon has two methyl groups.

parts.prompt: What is formed when ethene is shaken with cold, dilute, acidified potassium manganate(VII)?
parts.examinerComment: Mild oxidation adds two OH groups across the double bond. Hot concentrated manganate(VII) would break the C=C bond.

parts.prompt: Why is 2-bromopropane the major product when hydrogen bromide adds to propene?

options.text: The secondary carbocation intermediate is more stable than the primary carbocation.
Bromine is more electronegative than hydrogen.
The primary carbocation is formed more quickly.

markingPoints.text: A – The secondary carbocation intermediate is more stable than the primary carbocation.

parts.examinerComment: Alkyl groups donate electron density and stabilise the positive charge (Markovnikov addition).

parts.prompt: What volume of oxygen is needed to burn {v} cm³ of propane completely? All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
parts.examinerComment: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of moles.

parts.prompt: Which halogenoalkane is tertiary?
parts.examinerComment: In C the carbon bonded to bromine is attached to three other carbon atoms.

parts.prompt: Bromoethane is heated with sodium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol. What is the main organic product?
parts.examinerComment: In ethanol, OH⁻ acts mainly as a base and elimination of HBr occurs. Aqueous NaOH gives ethanol by substitution.

parts.prompt: Which conditions convert 1-bromopropane into propylamine?

options.text: excess ammonia in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube
KCN in ethanol, heated under reflux
dilute aqueous ammonia at room temperature

markingPoints.text: A – excess ammonia in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube

parts.examinerComment: Excess ammonia reduces further substitution; the sealed tube keeps the volatile ammonia in the mixture.

parts.prompt: What are the products when a small piece of sodium is added to ethanol?
parts.examinerComment: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. The reaction is less vigorous than sodium with water.

parts.prompt: Which alcohol is not oxidised when heated with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
parts.examinerComment: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol: there is no hydrogen atom on the carbon bearing the OH group.

parts.prompt: Which reagents convert ethanol into bromoethane?

options.text: sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid

markingPoints.text: B – sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid

parts.examinerComment: NaBr and concentrated H₂SO₄ produce HBr in situ, which substitutes the OH group.

parts.prompt: What is the organic product when propanal is reduced with NaBH₄?
parts.examinerComment: Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols; ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

parts.prompt: What is the mechanism of the reaction between hydrogen cyanide and ethanal, catalysed by KCN?
parts.examinerComment: The CN⁻ ion attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, then the intermediate gains a proton.

parts.prompt: Which compound gives a positive result with both Fehling's solution and alkaline aqueous iodine?
parts.examinerComment: Ethanal is an aldehyde and contains the CH₃CO– group needed for the tri-iodomethane test.

parts.prompt: Which conditions oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid?

options.text: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distilling off the product as it forms

markingPoints.text: A – acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heated under reflux

parts.examinerComment: Heating under reflux keeps the intermediate aldehyde in the flask so it is oxidised further.

parts.prompt: What are the products when ethanoic acid reacts with magnesium?
parts.examinerComment: Carboxylic acids react like other acids with reactive metals, producing a salt and hydrogen.

parts.prompt: Which is the structural formula of ethyl propanoate?
parts.examinerComment: The 'propanoate' part (CH₃CH₂COO–) comes from the acid and the 'ethyl' part from the alcohol.

parts.prompt: Which reagent reduces ethanenitrile to ethylamine?
parts.examinerComment: LiAlH₄ (or H₂ with a nickel catalyst) reduces C≡N to CH₂NH₂. Acid hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid.

parts.prompt: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile is heated under reflux with dilute sulfuric acid. What is the organic product?
parts.examinerComment: Acid hydrolysis converts the –CN group into –COOH; the OH group is unchanged.

parts.prompt: Why does an aqueous solution of ethylamine have a pH above 7?

options.text: The lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton from water, forming OH⁻ ions.
Ethylamine donates a proton to water.
Ethylamine reacts with water to form ammonia.

markingPoints.text: A – The lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton from water, forming OH⁻ ions.

parts.examinerComment: C₂H₅NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₅NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.

parts.prompt: Which monomer is used to make poly(chloroethene), PVC?
parts.examinerComment: The repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl– comes from chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl.

parts.prompt: A sample of poly(ethene) has an average relative molecular mass of {=28*n}. What is the average number of ethene monomer units in each polymer chain?
parts.examinerComment: Each ethene unit, C₂H₄, has Mᵣ = 28. Option B divides by the mass of a CH₂ group instead.

parts.prompt: Which statement about the disposal of poly(alkenes) is correct?

options.text: Poly(alkenes) are broken down quickly by bacteria in landfill.
Burning PVC can release toxic hydrogen chloride gas.
Poly(alkenes) dissolve slowly in rain water.

markingPoints.text: B – Burning PVC can release toxic hydrogen chloride gas.

parts.examinerComment: Poly(alkenes) are non-biodegradable; combustion of chlorinated polymers releases HCl.

parts.prompt: Which sequence of reagents converts 1-bromopropane into butanoic acid?

options.text: KCN in ethanol, then heat with dilute HCl(aq)

markingPoints.text: A – KCN in ethanol, then heat with dilute HCl(aq)

parts.examinerComment: The nitrile step adds one carbon atom; acid hydrolysis then gives the carboxylic acid. Option D gives an amine.

parts.prompt: Compound X reacts with sodium to give hydrogen. When X is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and the product is distilled off, the product gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. What is X?
parts.examinerComment: Only a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde on oxidation.

parts.prompt: Which reagent can be used to distinguish between ethanol and ethanoic acid?
parts.examinerComment: Only the carboxylic acid gives effervescence of CO₂. Both compounds react with sodium.

parts.prompt: Which infrared absorption range shows the O–H bond in a carboxylic acid?
parts.examinerComment: The hydrogen-bonded O–H in acids gives a very broad absorption; 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ is typical of alcohols.

parts.prompt: A compound contains one chlorine atom. What is the approximate ratio of the heights of the M and M+2 peaks in its mass spectrum?
parts.examinerComment: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl occur in roughly a 3 : 1 ratio. A 1 : 1 ratio indicates one bromine atom.

parts.prompt: The infrared spectrum of a compound has a strong absorption at 1710 cm⁻¹ and a very broad absorption from 2500 to 3000 cm⁻¹. Which compound is it?
parts.examinerComment: Both C=O and the broad acid O–H absorptions are present.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the number of unpaired electrons in a gaseous phosphorus atom in its ground state.
parts.examinerComment: The three 3p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus.

markingPoints.text: In sulfur, the electron removed is from a 3p orbital that already contains a pair of electrons
Repulsion between the paired electrons makes this electron easier to remove

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates wrongly referred to sulfur having more shielding; both electrons are in the same sub-shell.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {v1} cm³ of {c1} mol dm⁻³ aqueous sodium carbonate reacts exactly with {v2} cm³ of hydrochloric acid. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid, in mol dm⁻³.
parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers set out each step clearly. The most common error was ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A sample of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄•xH₂O, has a mass of {=round(a*(120.4+18.0*x)/120.4, 3)} g. After heating to constant mass, {a} g of anhydrous MgSO₄ remains. Calculate the value of x. (Mᵣ: MgSO₄ = 120.4, H₂O = 18.0)
parts.examinerComment: Candidates should give x as a whole number; the ratio of moles of water to moles of salt should be very close to it.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Predict the shape of a boron trifluoride molecule, BF₃, and state its bond angle. Explain why it has this shape.

markingPoints.text: Three bonding pairs and no lone pairs repel each other equally and get as far apart as possible

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates drew a lone pair on boron; boron has only three outer electrons.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium.

markingPoints.text: Magnesium has more delocalised electrons per atom / Mg²⁺ ions have a greater charge (and are smaller)
so the electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons is stronger

parts.examinerComment: Answers referring to 'stronger intermolecular forces' gained no credit: metals have metallic bonding.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {m} g of a volatile liquid is vaporised at {T} K. The vapour occupies {V} cm³ at a pressure of {p} Pa. Calculate the Mᵣ of the liquid. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

markingPoints.text: M1 for converting the volume: {V} cm³ = {=V*1e-6} m³

parts.examinerComment: The commonest error was leaving the volume in cm³, giving an answer 10⁶ times too large.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Suggest why the ideal gas equation gives a less accurate result for ammonia than for helium at room temperature.

markingPoints.text: Ammonia molecules have (hydrogen bonding / stronger) intermolecular forces; helium has only very weak forces
Ammonia molecules are larger, so their own volume is less negligible

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers related each point to an assumption of the ideal gas model.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {m} g of propan-1-ol (Mᵣ = 60.0) is burned and the energy released heats {w} g of water. The temperature of the water rises by {=round(H*1000*m/(60*w*4.18), 1)} °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol, in kJ mol⁻¹. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)

markingPoints.text: A1 for ΔHc = {=-w*4.18*round(H*1000*m/(60*w*4.18), 1)*60/(m*1000)} kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign required)

parts.examinerComment: Answers without a negative sign, or not converted from J to kJ, lost the final mark.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The value obtained in this type of experiment is much less exothermic than the data book value. Suggest two reasons.

markingPoints.text: Heat is lost to the surroundings / heats the container rather than the water
Some fuel evaporates from the wick before burning

parts.examinerComment: Vague answers such as 'human error' were not credited.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A solution containing iron(II) ions is titrated with {c} mol dm⁻³ acidified potassium manganate(VII). {v} cm³ is needed to reach the end-point. MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. Calculate the mass of iron(II) in the solution, in g. (Aᵣ: Fe = 55.8)
parts.examinerComment: Many candidates used a 1 : 1 ratio; the balanced equation must always be used.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Acidified dichromate(VI) ions, Cr₂O₇²⁻, oxidise Fe²⁺ ions to Fe³⁺ ions and are reduced to Cr³⁺ ions. Construct the overall ionic equation for this reaction.

markingPoints.text: Half-equations: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻

parts.examinerComment: Check that both atoms and charges balance in the final equation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {a} mol of ethanoic acid and {b} mol of ethanol are mixed with a little acid catalyst and left to reach equilibrium. CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. At equilibrium the mixture contains {=round((K*(a+b) - sqrt(K^2*(a+b)^2 - 4*(K-1)*K*a*b))/(2*(K-1)), 2)} mol of ethyl ethanoate. Calculate Kc.

markingPoints.text: M1 for equilibrium moles: acid = {=a-round((K*(a+b) - sqrt(K^2*(a+b)^2 - 4*(K-1)*K*a*b))/(2*(K-1)), 2)}, alcohol = {=b-round((K*(a+b) - sqrt(K^2*(a+b)^2 - 4*(K-1)*K*a*b))/(2*(K-1)), 2)}, ester = water = {=round((K*(a+b) - sqrt(K^2*(a+b)^2 - 4*(K-1)*K*a*b))/(2*(K-1)), 2)}
M1 for Kc = [ester][water] / ([acid][alcohol]); the volumes cancel

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers stated that the volume cancels because there are equal numbers of moles on each side.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Dinitrogen tetraoxide dissociates: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). An equilibrium mixture contains {n1} mol of N₂O₄ and {n2} mol of NO₂ at a total pressure of {P} kPa. Calculate Kp, in kPa.

markingPoints.text: M1 for mole fractions: N₂O₄ = {=n1/(n1+n2)}, NO₂ = {=n2/(n1+n2)}
M1 for partial pressures: N₂O₄ = {=n1/(n1+n2)*P} kPa, NO₂ = {=n2/(n1+n2)*P} kPa
A1 for Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄) = {=(n2/(n1+n2)*P)^2/(n1/(n1+n2)*P)} kPa

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates used the moles directly instead of partial pressures.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Magnesium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid. {v} cm³ of hydrogen is collected in the first {t} s. Calculate the mean rate of production of hydrogen over this time, in mol s⁻¹. (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³ at room conditions.)
parts.examinerComment: Answers can be typed in standard form, e.g. 3.33e-5.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use collision theory to explain why the reaction is faster when more concentrated hydrochloric acid is used.

markingPoints.text: More acid particles (H⁺ ions) per unit volume
so more frequent collisions, and therefore more frequent successful collisions with energy ≥ Eₐ

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers referred to frequency of collisions rather than simply 'more collisions'.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write an equation for the reaction of silicon(IV) chloride with water and state the approximate pH of the resulting mixture.
parts.examinerComment: Many candidates correctly described white fumes of HCl. Accept SiCl₄ + 4H₂O → Si(OH)₄ + 4HCl.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe and explain the variation in electrical conductivity of the elements sodium, aluminium and silicon.

markingPoints.text: Conductivity increases from Na to Al
because the number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (1, 2, 3)
Silicon is a semiconductor / has low conductivity because it has a giant covalent structure with no (few) delocalised electrons

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers described silicon as metallic.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {m} g of calcium carbonate is heated to constant mass. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide formed, in g. (Mᵣ: CaCO₃ = 100.1, CaO = 56.1)
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the first ionisation energy decreases down Group 2.

markingPoints.text: The outer electron is further from the nucleus / the atomic radius increases
and there is more shielding by inner shells, which outweighs the increase in nuclear charge

parts.examinerComment: The increase in nuclear charge must be mentioned as being outweighed for full credit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium bromide. Describe what is seen, write an ionic equation and explain the reaction in terms of oxidising power.

markingPoints.text: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it oxidises bromide ions

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates wrote 'brown' for bromine: orange or yellow is expected in aqueous solution.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Chlorine is used to treat drinking water. Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine with water and give the oxidation number of chlorine in each product.
parts.examinerComment: This is another example of disproportionation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write an equation for the reaction of ammonia with sulfuric acid to make the fertiliser ammonium sulfate.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why ammonium fertilisers should not be spread on fields at the same time as lime, calcium hydroxide.

markingPoints.text: Hydroxide ions react with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O
so nitrogen is lost from the soil / the fertiliser becomes less effective

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers included the ionic equation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Give the general formula of the alkanes.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Define the term nucleophile and give one example.

markingPoints.text: A species that donates a pair of electrons (to form a covalent bond)

parts.examinerComment: 'Attracted to positive charge' alone was not enough for the definition mark.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between ethene and bromine. Your answer should describe the movement of electrons and name the intermediate.

markingPoints.text: Br₂ is polarised by the π electrons; the π electrons attack Brδ+
The Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming a carbocation and Br⁻

parts.examinerComment: This is electrophilic addition. Curly arrows must start from a bond or a lone pair.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Decane, C₁₀H₂₂, is cracked to give octane and one other product. Write an equation and state one condition used.

markingPoints.text: High temperature, or a zeolite / Al₂O₃ catalyst

parts.examinerComment: Cracking always produces at least one alkene.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the SN2 mechanism for the reaction of bromoethane with hydroxide ions.

markingPoints.text: Lone pair on OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon bonded to Br
Transition state with partial bonds to both OH and Br (five groups around carbon)
C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, releasing Br⁻ and forming ethanol

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should state that the attack happens from the side opposite the bromine.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were once widely used as refrigerants. Explain why they were used and why their use is now restricted.

markingPoints.text: They are unreactive / non-toxic / non-flammable (because of strong C–F and C–Cl bonds)
In the upper atmosphere, UV breaks C–Cl bonds giving Cl radicals which catalyse ozone depletion

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers linked the unreactivity to long lifetimes in the atmosphere.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Butan-2-ol gives a positive result when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine. State what is seen and the structural feature responsible.
parts.examinerComment: Ethanol is the only primary alcohol with this group.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give the reagent and conditions for the dehydration of ethanol, and name the organic product.

markingPoints.text: Heat with Al₂O₃ (or excess concentrated H₂SO₄ / H₃PO₄)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Propanal reacts with HCN in the presence of KCN to form 2-hydroxybutanenitrile. Explain why the product is a racemic mixture.

markingPoints.text: The product has a chiral centre
The C=O group is planar (trigonal planar carbon)
CN⁻ can attack from either side with equal probability, giving equal amounts of each enantiomer

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates knew the answer was 'racemic' but did not explain why.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Name the product formed when propanone reacts with HCN in the presence of KCN.
parts.examinerComment: Count the carbons carefully: the nitrile carbon is included in the name.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {m} g of ethanoic acid (Mᵣ = 60.0) is heated with excess ethanol and a catalyst. {=round(m*88/60*p/100, 2)} g of ethyl ethanoate (Mᵣ = 88.0) is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.

markingPoints.text: M1 for theoretical mass of ester = {=m*88/60} g

parts.examinerComment: Yields below 100% are expected for a reversible reaction.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the conditions used for this esterification and explain why the yield is less than 100%.

markingPoints.text: The reaction is reversible / reaches equilibrium (or loss on purification)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Bromoethane is heated with ammonia. Explain why a mixture of products forms and how the yield of ethylamine can be increased.

markingPoints.text: Ethylamine is also a nucleophile, so it reacts with more bromoethane to give secondary/tertiary amines

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers named diethylamine as a further product.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Name the organic product formed when propanenitrile is reduced with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst.
parts.examinerComment: Reduction of a nitrile keeps the same number of carbon atoms.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Give the repeat unit of poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE.
parts.examinerComment: Show the bonds extending at each end of the repeat unit.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A polymer has the repeat unit –CH₂–CH(CN)–. Give the structure of the monomer and state the type of polymerisation.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Outline a two-step synthesis of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid from ethanal. Give reagents and conditions for each step and name the intermediate.

markingPoints.text: Step 1: HCN with KCN catalyst (room temperature)
Step 2: heat under reflux with dilute acid (e.g. HCl(aq))

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers used KCN in ethanol, which is used for halogenoalkanes, not carbonyl compounds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compound Y, C₃H₆O, gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but does not react with Tollens' reagent. Identify Y and explain your reasoning.

markingPoints.text: 2,4-DNPH shows a carbonyl group; no reaction with Tollens' shows it is not an aldehyde, so a ketone

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Compound Z has a molecular ion peak at m/e = 58. Its infrared spectrum shows a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no absorption between 2500 and 3600 cm⁻¹. Suggest a structure for Z, explaining your reasoning.

markingPoints.text: No absorption at 2500–3600 cm⁻¹ shows there is no O–H
Mᵣ = 58 fits C₃H₆O, e.g. propanone CH₃COCH₃ (or propanal)

parts.examinerComment: Use all the evidence given.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Suggest the formula of the ion responsible for the peak at m/e = 29 in the mass spectrum of propanal.
parts.examinerComment: Fragment ions must carry a positive charge.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Use the following data to calculate the lattice energy of a Group 1 chloride, MCl, in kJ mol⁻¹. Enthalpy change of formation of MCl(s) = −{f} kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy change of atomisation of M = +{a} kJ mol⁻¹; first ionisation energy of M = +{i} kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy change of atomisation of chlorine = +122 kJ mol⁻¹; first electron affinity of chlorine = −349 kJ mol⁻¹.

markingPoints.text: M1 for a correct Born–Haber relationship: ΔHf = ΔHat(M) + IE + ΔHat(Cl) + EA + LE

parts.examinerComment: Most errors came from using the bond energy of Cl₂ (242) instead of the atomisation enthalpy (122).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the standard entropy change, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). Standard entropies, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: N₂(g) 191.6; H₂(g) 130.6; NH₃(g) 192.3.
parts.examinerComment: The negative value fits the decrease from four moles of gas to two.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For the Haber process reaction, ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG at {T} K, in kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Above about 460 K, ΔG becomes positive and the reaction is no longer feasible under standard conditions.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why the lattice energy of magnesium oxide is much more exothermic than that of sodium chloride.

markingPoints.text: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have larger charges than Na⁺ and Cl⁻
so the electrostatic attraction between the ions is much stronger

parts.examinerComment: Answers should compare both charge and ionic radius.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Solid ammonium nitrate dissolves in water endothermically. Explain, in terms of entropy, why it dissolves spontaneously at room temperature.

markingPoints.text: ΔS (of the system) is positive because ions in solution are more disordered than in the lattice
TΔS is greater than ΔH, so ΔG is negative

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers referred to ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the time, in minutes, needed to deposit {m} g of silver at the cathode using a current of {I} A. Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. (Aᵣ: Ag = 107.9; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
parts.examinerComment: Remember to convert seconds into minutes at the end.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: In an experiment to find the Avogadro constant, a current of {I} A is passed through aqueous copper(II) sulfate for {t} minutes. The cathode gains {=round(I*t*60*63.5/(2*96500), 3)} g. Calculate a value for the Avogadro constant, L. (Aᵣ: Cu = 63.5; charge on one electron = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
parts.examinerComment: Answers can be typed in standard form, e.g. 6.02e23. The number of electrons is Q ÷ e.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the electrode potential of the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ half-cell (E° = +0.77 V) when [Fe³⁺] = {a} mol dm⁻³ and [Fe²⁺] = {b} mol dm⁻³, in V. E = E° + 0.059 log([Fe³⁺]/[Fe²⁺])
parts.examinerComment: z = 1 for this half-cell.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Name the product at each electrode and write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.examinerComment: Sodium is not discharged because water is more easily reduced (E° of Na⁺/Na is very negative).

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: E°(MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺) = +1.52 V and E°(Cl₂/Cl⁻) = +1.36 V. Explain why dilute hydrochloric acid is not used to acidify potassium manganate(VII) in titrations.

markingPoints.text: E°cell = 1.52 − 1.36 = +0.16 V, positive, so MnO₄⁻ can oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂
so some manganate(VII) is used up by the acid and the titre is too large

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers calculated E°cell.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the pH of {c} mol dm⁻³ aqueous sodium hydroxide at 298 K. (Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶)
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A {c} mol dm⁻³ solution of a weak monobasic acid, HA, has a pH of {=round(-log10(sqrt(K*1e-5*c)), 2)}. Calculate the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of HA.
parts.examinerComment: Assume [H⁺] = [A⁻] and that [HA] at equilibrium equals the initial concentration.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The solubility product of lead(II) iodide, PbI₂, is {k} × 10⁻⁹ mol³ dm⁻⁹. Calculate the solubility of PbI₂, in mol dm⁻³.
parts.examinerComment: The most common error was writing Ksp = s² or 2s³.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: {m} g of compound X is dissolved in 100 cm³ of water. The solution is shaken with {v} cm³ of hexane until equilibrium is reached. The partition coefficient of X between hexane and water, Kpc = [X in hexane]/[X in water], is {K}. Calculate the mass of X extracted into the hexane, in g.
parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers wrote the expression in terms of x and then rearranged it.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain how a solution containing ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate controls pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added. Include equations.

markingPoints.text: Large reservoirs of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻
Added H⁺ reacts with ethanoate: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH
Added OH⁻ reacts with the acid: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O, so [H⁺] stays almost constant

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers stated that the buffer 'neutralises' acid without equations.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A reaction has the rate equation rate = k[A]²[B]. When [A] = {a} mol dm⁻³ and [B] = {b} mol dm⁻³, the initial rate is {r} × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Calculate the rate constant, k, in dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Remember to square [A]. Answers can be typed in standard form.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A substance decomposes in a first-order reaction with a half-life of {h} minutes. Calculate the mass remaining after {=n*h} minutes if the initial mass is {m} g.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A reaction has an activation energy of {E} kJ mol⁻¹. Use the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT), to calculate how many times larger the rate constant is at {=298+d} K than at 298 K. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
parts.examinerComment: Eₐ must be converted into J mol⁻¹ to match the units of R.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The reaction NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) is thought to occur in two steps: step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. Deduce the rate equation and explain your answer.

markingPoints.text: Step 1 is the rate-determining step and involves two NO₂ molecules
CO is not involved until after the rate-determining step, so it is zero order

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates wrongly wrote the rate equation from the overall equation.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Iron(II) ions catalyse the reaction between peroxodisulfate ions, S₂O₈²⁻, and iodide ions. Write two equations to show how Fe²⁺ acts as a catalyst.
parts.examinerComment: The catalyst works because both steps involve oppositely charged ions; the direct reaction involves two negative ions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For a Group 2 sulfate, MSO₄: lattice energy = −{L} kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy change of hydration of M²⁺ = −{h} kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy change of hydration of SO₄²⁻ = −1080 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of MSO₄, in kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: The lattice energy is reversed in the cycle because the lattice is broken up.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group. Explain this trend in terms of lattice energy and enthalpy change of hydration.

markingPoints.text: Down the group the cation radius increases, so both lattice energy and hydration enthalpy become less exothermic
Lattice energy decreases more than hydration enthalpy (hydroxide ion is small, so the lattice energy depends strongly on cation size)
so ΔHsol becomes more exothermic / less endothermic and solubility increases

parts.examinerComment: Contrast this with the sulfates, where the large anion means hydration enthalpy changes more.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: {m} g of calcium nitrate is heated until decomposition is complete. 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Calculate the total volume of gas produced, measured at room conditions, in cm³. (Mᵣ Ca(NO₃)₂ = 164.1; 1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³)
parts.examinerComment: Both NO₂ and O₂ must be counted: 5 mol of gas from 2 mol of nitrate.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Name the brown gas produced when Group 2 nitrates are heated.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Suggest whether magnesium nitrate or strontium nitrate decomposes at a lower temperature. Explain your answer.

markingPoints.text: Mg²⁺ is smaller and so has a higher charge density
so it polarises (distorts) the nitrate ion more, weakening the N–O bonds

parts.examinerComment: Answers must refer to polarisation of the anion, not of the cation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {m} g of impure iron wire is dissolved in excess dilute sulfuric acid to give Fe²⁺ ions, and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. A 25.0 cm³ portion needs {=round(p/100*m/55.8/10/6/c*1000, 2)} cm³ of {c} mol dm⁻³ potassium dichromate(VI) for complete reaction. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in the wire. (Aᵣ: Fe = 55.8)

markingPoints.text: M1 for moles Fe²⁺ in 25.0 cm³ = 6 × moles of dichromate
M1 for scaling × 10 and × 55.8 to give mass of iron = {=round(p/100*m/55.8/10/6/c*1000, 2)*c/1000*6*10*55.8} g

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates forgot to scale up from the 25.0 cm³ portion to the 250 cm³ solution.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Aqueous ammonia is added dropwise, and then in excess, to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Describe what is seen and give the formula of the copper-containing species formed at each stage.

markingPoints.text: Dissolves to give a deep (dark) blue solution

parts.examinerComment: The second stage is a ligand exchange reaction.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: 1,2-diaminoethane, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂, forms two dative bonds to a metal ion. What type of ligand is it?
parts.examinerComment: Each nitrogen atom donates one lone pair.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why transition elements can show a variety of oxidation states.

markingPoints.text: The 3d and 4s orbitals/electrons are close in energy
so different numbers of electrons can be lost (or used in bonding) for similar amounts of energy

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Deduce the oxidation number of iron in the complex ion [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻.
parts.examinerComment: Six cyanide ligands each carry a 1− charge: x − 6 = −3.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: How many optical isomers does 3-methylhexane have?
parts.examinerComment: Carbon 3 is bonded to H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇, so it is a chiral centre.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain what is meant by a racemic mixture and why it has no effect on plane-polarised light.

markingPoints.text: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers
The rotations of plane-polarised light by each enantiomer are equal and opposite, so they cancel

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Name the compound C₆H₅CH₃.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State the two structural features that together make a carbon atom a chiral centre, and state the relationship between the two optical isomers.

markingPoints.text: A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups
The isomers are non-superimposable mirror images

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State the hybridisation of the carbon atoms in benzene.
parts.examinerComment: Each carbon uses three sp² orbitals for σ bonds; the remaining p orbitals overlap to form the delocalised π system.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between benzene and bromine in the presence of FeBr₃. Include an equation for the formation of the electrophile.

markingPoints.text: π electrons of the ring attack Br⁺, forming a positively charged intermediate
The intermediate loses H⁺ to restore the delocalised ring

parts.examinerComment: This is electrophilic substitution. The stability of the delocalised ring is restored in the final step.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Name the organic product formed when methylbenzene is heated under reflux with alkaline potassium manganate(VII) and the mixture is then acidified.
parts.examinerComment: The whole side chain is oxidised to –COOH.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in two different ways. State the conditions needed for substitution in the side chain and for substitution in the ring.

markingPoints.text: Ring: AlCl₃ (or FeCl₃) catalyst, no UV

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: {m} g of benzene (Mᵣ = 78.0) is nitrated and {=round(m*123/78*p/100, 2)} g of nitrobenzene (Mᵣ = 123.0) is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Electrophilic substitution of methylbenzene occurs mainly at which ring positions, relative to the methyl group?
parts.examinerComment: The methyl group is 2,4-directing.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the SN1 mechanism for the hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by aqueous hydroxide ions, and explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes react by this mechanism.

markingPoints.text: The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to form a carbocation and Br⁻ (slow step)
The tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups
and the bulky groups hinder attack from the back (SN2)

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should identify the rate-determining step.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the order of reaction with respect to hydroxide ions for the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
parts.examinerComment: OH⁻ is not involved in the rate-determining step.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed. Explain why an SN2 reaction gives a single optically active product while an SN1 reaction gives a racemic mixture.

markingPoints.text: SN2: the nucleophile always attacks from the side opposite the C–Br bond, so the configuration is inverted (single enantiomer)
SN1: the carbocation intermediate is planar
so attack from either side is equally likely, giving equal amounts of each enantiomer

parts.examinerComment: Good answers referred to the geometry of the intermediate.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Suggest why 1-bromobutane is hydrolysed by an SN2 mechanism rather than SN1.

markingPoints.text: A primary carbocation would be very unstable (only one alkyl group)
There is little steric hindrance to attack by the nucleophile

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Write the rate equation for the SN2 hydrolysis of bromoethane by hydroxide ions.
parts.examinerComment: Both species are involved in the single step.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate to give carbon dioxide, but phenol does not. What does this show about the acidity of phenol? Explain your answer.

markingPoints.text: Phenol is a weaker acid than ethanoic acid (and than carbonic acid)
It does not produce a high enough [H⁺] to release CO₂ from carbonate

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Write an equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature but benzene does not.

markingPoints.text: A lone pair on the oxygen atom is delocalised into the ring
increasing the electron density of the ring
so the ring polarises bromine more strongly / is more readily attacked by electrophiles

parts.examinerComment: The product is 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a white precipitate.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Name an organic product formed when phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid at room temperature.
parts.examinerComment: Benzene needs concentrated acids to be nitrated; phenol does not.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Place ethanol, phenol and water in order of increasing acidity and explain the position of ethanol and of phenol.

markingPoints.text: Ethanol: the ethyl group donates electrons, destabilising the ethoxide ion
Phenol: the negative charge of the phenoxide ion is delocalised into the ring, stabilising it

parts.examinerComment: Explanations should refer to the stability of the anion.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: {m} g of ethanoyl chloride (Mᵣ = 78.5) is added to excess water. CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl. Calculate the volume of {c} mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide needed to neutralise all the acid formed, in cm³.
parts.examinerComment: Both ethanoic acid and hydrochloric acid are neutralised.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why ethanoyl chloride is hydrolysed much more readily than chloroethane.

markingPoints.text: In ethanoyl chloride the carbon is bonded to both O and Cl
so it carries a larger δ+ charge
and is more easily attacked by nucleophiles such as water (the C=O also allows addition–elimination)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Name the organic product formed when ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol.
parts.examinerComment: This reaction is faster than esterification with the acid and is not reversible.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Name a reagent that converts ethanoic acid into ethanoyl chloride and name the inorganic products.

markingPoints.text: SO₂ and HCl (or POCl₃ and HCl / H₃PO₃)

parts.examinerComment: The products must match the reagent.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Describe a test that distinguishes methanoic acid from ethanoic acid. Explain why methanoic acid reacts.

markingPoints.text: Warm with Tollens' reagent: silver mirror with methanoic acid only (or Fehling's: red precipitate; or acidified KMnO₄: decolourised)
Methanoic acid contains an H–C=O group / can be oxidised (to CO₂ and water)

parts.examinerComment: Ethanoic acid cannot be oxidised further by these reagents.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe how an azo dye is made from benzenediazonium chloride and phenol. Give the conditions and state what is seen.

markingPoints.text: Phenol dissolved in aqueous NaOH (alkaline solution)

parts.examinerComment: Diazonium salts decompose above about 10 °C.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Name the reagents used to reduce nitrobenzene to phenylamine.

markingPoints.text: Tin and concentrated HCl (followed by NaOH)

parts.examinerComment: Aqueous NaOH is added afterwards to release the free amine.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A polypeptide is formed from {n} glycine molecules (Mᵣ of glycine = 75.0) joined by peptide bonds. Calculate the Mᵣ of the polypeptide. (Mᵣ: H₂O = 18.0)
parts.examinerComment: A chain of n amino acids contains n − 1 peptide bonds.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why amino acids are solids with relatively high melting points.

markingPoints.text: with strong ionic attractions between the charged groups of neighbouring molecules

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Ethanamide is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Name the products.
parts.examinerComment: Amides are hydrolysed by both acids and alkalis.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The polyester PET is made from two monomers. Name or give the structures of the two monomers.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The repeat unit of nylon-6,6 has Mᵣ = 226. A sample of nylon-6,6 has an average Mᵣ of {=226*n}. Calculate the average number of repeat units in each chain.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why Kevlar, an aromatic polyamide, is very strong.

markingPoints.text: Rigid, linear chains that line up parallel to each other
Strong hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups on neighbouring chains

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Name the linkage that joins amino acid residues in a protein.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Poly(lactic acid) is described as biodegradable. Explain why it can be broken down while poly(propene) cannot.

markingPoints.text: Poly(lactic acid) contains ester linkages that can be hydrolysed (by water / enzymes / bacteria)
Poly(propene) has only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds which are not attacked

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Outline a two-step synthesis of 4-nitrobenzoic acid from methylbenzene. Give reagents and conditions for each step.

markingPoints.text: Step 1: concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄
at about 30 °C (to give 4-nitromethylbenzene, separated from the 2-isomer)
Step 2: hot alkaline KMnO₄ under reflux

parts.examinerComment: Nitrating first uses the 2,4-directing effect of the methyl group; the –COOH group would direct to position 3.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give the reagents and conditions for converting benzene into phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃.
parts.examinerComment: This is Friedel–Crafts acylation.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Suggest two methods that a pharmaceutical company could use to make a single enantiomer of a chiral drug rather than a racemic mixture.

markingPoints.text: Use a chiral catalyst or an enzyme
Start from a naturally occurring single enantiomer (chiral pool)
Separate (resolve) the enantiomers from a racemic mixture

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A three-step synthesis has yields of {a}%, {b}% and {c}% for the three steps. Calculate the overall percentage yield.
parts.examinerComment: Yields multiply; they are not added or averaged.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Name the functional group formed when phenylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride.
